sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: Joshua had died.{a} Then the Israelites asked Yahweh, “Which tribe should go first to fight the Canaanites for us?”
Yahweh replied, “Judah. I have already put the land in their hands.”
Judah told his brother tribe Simeon, “Join me in the land that fell to me, and we will fight the Canaanites together. After that, I will go with you into your land.” So Simeon went along.
Judah attacked, and Yahweh gave them the Canaanites and the Perizzites. At Bezek they struck down ten thousand men.
At Bezek they came across Adoni-bezek{b} and attacked him. The Canaanites and the Perizzites were beaten.
Adoni-bezek tried to escape. Judah’s men hunted him, caught him, and cut off both his thumbs and both his big toes.

“Seventy kings I once left without thumbs or big toes,” said Adoni-bezek. “They searched for scraps under my table. God has now done the same to me.” Judah’s men brought him to Jerusalem, and that is where he died.
Judah’s army fought Jerusalem and seized it. They killed its people by the sword and burned the town.
Afterward Judah’s army went down and fought the Canaanites in the hills, in the Negev,{c} and in the western foothills.
Next they went after the Canaanites of Hebron, a town once known as Kiriath-arba.{d} They beat Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
From there they went against the people of Debir, a town earlier named Kiriath-sepher.{e}
Caleb announced, “Any man who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it will get my daughter Achsah as his bride.”
Caleb’s younger brother Othniel{f}, son of Kenaz, took the town. As a result Caleb gave Othniel his daughter Achsah as his wife.
On the day Achsah married Othniel, she pushed him to ask her father for a field. As she slid off her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What is it you want?”
“A favor, please,” she said. “The land you gave me is dry, in the Negev. Give me pools of water as well.” And Caleb gave her both the upper pools and the lower pools.{g}
The descendants of Moses’ father-in-law, a Kenite,{h} had left the City of Palms{i} with Judah’s people. They went to the desert of Judah, in the Negev near Arad, and settled there among the people.
Judah went with their brother tribe Simeon. Together they beat the Canaanites living at Zephath and destroyed the town completely.{j} They named it Hormah.
Judah also took Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, each with the land around it.{k}
Yahweh stood by Judah, so Judah took over the hill country. The people of the coastal plain, however, had iron chariots,{l} and Judah could not force them out.
Hebron went to Caleb, just as Moses had said. Caleb forced out the three sons of Anak who had lived in it.
In Jerusalem, the Jebusites were never forced out by the Benjaminites. Jebusites and Benjaminites still share that town today.
Joseph’s tribes marched against Bethel too, and Yahweh was with them.
The tribe sent men to spy out Bethel, a town once called Luz.
The spies spotted a man walking out of the town. “Show us the way in,” they said, “and we will be kind to you.”
So he pointed out the way into the town. Joseph’s tribes killed everyone in it with their swords. Only that man and his family were set free.
He moved to the land of the Hittites, built a town, and called it Luz. That name has stuck to this day.
The tribe of Manasseh never took over Beth-shean and its villages,{m} or Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, and Megiddo with their villages. The Canaanites held on stubbornly to that region.
In time Israel grew strong, and the Canaanites were put to forced labor. Even so, Israel never pushed them out for good.
Ephraim’s people never forced the Canaanites out of Gezer. Canaanites went on living there beside them.
Zebulun failed to throw out those living in Kitron and Nahalol. Canaanites remained in those towns and did forced labor for Zebulun.
Asher also failed to push out the people of Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob.
For that reason, Asher’s people made their homes among the Canaanites who held the land. They had never forced them out.
Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath were not emptied by Naphtali. Naphtali’s people settled among the Canaanites of that land, though the townspeople of those two places did forced labor for Naphtali.
The Amorites squeezed the tribe of Dan into the hills. They would not allow Dan to go down into the plain.
The Amorites kept Har-heres,{n} Aijalon, and Shaalbim. But Joseph’s tribes grew stronger and made them work for Israel.
The Amorites’{o} border ran from the Akrabbim Pass,{p} from Sela, and on up.

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament of Judges survives in two main forms, the B text (Codex Vaticanus and related manuscripts) and the A text (Codex Alexandrinus and related manuscripts). They often differ in wording and sometimes in meaning. Important differences are noted. Joshua means “Yahweh is salvation.”
Adoni-bezek means “lord of Bezek.”
The Negev is the dry southern region of Judah. The word also means “south.”
Kiriath-arba means “city of Arba” or “city of four.” Hebron perhaps means “alliance.”
Kiriath-sepher means “town of the book” or “town of the scribe.”
Othniel perhaps means “my strength is God” or “lion of God.” The meaning is uncertain.
Or “Gulloth-illith and Gulloth-tahtith.” Gulloth means “basins” or “pools.” Compare Joshua 15:16-19.
The Greek Old Testament (B text) names him: “the sons of Jothor (Jethro) the Kenite.” Compare 4:11, which calls Moses’ father-in-law Hobab.
That is, Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3).
Hebrew charam, to give something over completely to God, usually by destroying it. Hormah sounds like the word for “given over to destruction.”

The Greek Old Testament says the opposite: “But Judah did not take Gaza and its land, or Ashkelon and its land, or Ekron and its land, or Ashdod and the land around it.” This fits verse 19 and the later history of the Philistine towns.
Hebrew rekeb barzel. The Greek Old Testament (B text) takes rekeb as a name: “because Rechab stopped them.”
Hebrew “daughters,” the usual word for the smaller towns that depend on a city. It is used this way all through this verse.
Har-heres means “mountain of the sun.” Compare Ir-shemesh (“city of the sun”) in Joshua 19:41.
Some Greek manuscripts and many scholars read “Edomites,” which fits the place of the Akrabbim Pass.
Akrabbim means “scorpions.” Sela means “rock.”

verses.text: Yahweh’s messenger traveled from Gilgal up to Bochim.{a} “Out of Egypt I led you,” he said, “into the land I swore to give your ancestors. I said that I would never break my covenant with you.
I also said you must make no agreements with the people of this land, and that you must destroy their altars. Yet you ignored me. How could you do this?
So now I tell you this: I will not drive these people out ahead of you. They will be thorns in your sides,{b} and their gods will trap you.”
The messenger finished speaking to all the Israelites, and the people began to sob out loud.
They called the place Bochim, and there they made sacrifices to Yahweh.
Joshua sent the people away, and each tribe went to take the land it had been given.
The people served Yahweh all through Joshua’s life. They kept it up while the elders lived who outlasted Joshua and had seen the great things Yahweh did for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, Yahweh’s servant, died at 110 years of age.
They buried him in the land that was his own, at Timnath-heres,{c} in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
In time, everyone from that generation had died. The next generation had never known Yahweh or his work for Israel.
They did evil things before Yahweh by serving the Baals.{d}
They deserted Yahweh, the God of their ancestors, the one who rescued them from Egypt. Instead they followed the gods of nearby peoples, bowed to them, and made Yahweh furious.
They left Yahweh and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.{e}
Yahweh’s anger flared up against Israel. He handed them over to robbers who took everything they had. He sold them to the enemies all around, and Israel could no longer stand up to them.
Everywhere the Israelites went, Yahweh’s hand worked against them. He had warned them, and he had made them a promise. Now they were in terrible trouble.
Then Yahweh sent judges,{f} who rescued them from the people who robbed them.

But the Israelites would not listen even to their judges. They chased after other gods as if they were unfaithful to a husband, and they bowed down to them. Their ancestors had obeyed Yahweh’s commands, but the Israelites quickly left that road. They would not walk it.

Each time Yahweh gave them a judge, he was with that judge. As long as the judge lived, Yahweh saved the people from their enemies. He felt sorry for them when they groaned under those who hurt and crushed them.

Yet each time a judge died, the people slid back into their old ways. They were even worse than their ancestors. They followed other gods, served them, and bowed down to them. They refused to quit their evil habits or their stubbornness.
So Yahweh burned with anger at Israel. He said, “This nation has broken the covenant I commanded their ancestors to keep, and they have ignored me.
From now on I will not drive out the nations that Joshua left behind when he died.
They will be my test for Israel. I want to see whether Israel will walk in Yahweh’s way, as their ancestors did.”
That is why Yahweh left those nations in the land. He did not drive them out quickly, and he never gave them to Joshua.

notes.text: Bochim means “weepers” (verse 5). The Greek Old Testament adds “and to Bethel and to the house of Israel.”

Hebrew “they will be sides to you.” “Thorns in” comes from similar warnings in Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13. The Greek Old Testament reads “they will be troubles to you,” and the Latin Vulgate reads “enemies.”
Timnath-heres means “portion of the sun.” In Joshua 19:50 and 24:30 the name is Timnath-serah (“leftover portion”), with two letters swapped.
Baal means “lord” or “master,” the title of the Canaanite storm god. The plural means the local forms of his worship.
Ashtaroth is the plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war.
Hebrew shophetim, leaders who rescued Israel and ruled it, not only judges in a court of law.

verses.text: These are the nations Yahweh left in the land to test Israel, all those who had never fought in the wars of Canaan.
He did it so that Israel’s later generations would learn about war, those who had never known it before.
These were the five Philistine rulers,{a} every Canaanite, the Sidonians, and the Hivites of the Lebanon hills, from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath.{b}
They were there as a test. Would Israel keep the commands Yahweh gave their ancestors through Moses?
So Israelites settled among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
They took those peoples’ daughters as wives, gave their own daughters to those peoples’ sons, and began to serve their gods.
Israel did evil in Yahweh’s sight. They forgot Yahweh their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.{c}
Yahweh was angry with Israel and sold them to Cushan-rishathaim,{d} king of Aram-naharaim.{e} Israel served him eight years.
When the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, he sent them a rescuer, Othniel. His father was Kenaz, and his uncle was Caleb.
Yahweh’s Spirit came on Othniel, and he became Israel’s judge. He went to war, and Yahweh handed Cushan-rishathaim, king of Aram, over to him. Othniel beat him.
For forty years the land was at rest. Then Othniel died.
Once more Israel did evil in Yahweh’s sight. So Yahweh gave Eglon,{f} king of Moab, power over Israel, because of their evil.
Eglon brought the Ammonites and the Amalekites together, attacked Israel, and took the City of Palms.
For eighteen years Israel was under Eglon, king of Moab.

Again the Israelites called to Yahweh for help, and he sent them a rescuer. His name was Ehud,{g} the left-handed{h} son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin. Israel used him to carry their tribute to King Eglon of Moab.
Ehud forged a sword for himself with two sharp edges, about a foot{i} long. He tied it under his clothes on his right thigh.
He handed the tribute to Eglon, who ruled Moab and was a very fat man.
When Ehud had handed over the tribute, he sent away the men who had carried it.
But at the carved stones{j} near Gilgal, Ehud turned back. “Your Majesty, I bring you a secret message,” he said. “Be quiet!” said the king, and everyone standing near him left.
Ehud walked up to him while he sat alone in his cool upstairs room. “God has sent me with a message for you,” he said. The king rose from his seat.
Ehud’s left hand shot out, drew the sword from his right thigh, and drove it into the king’s belly.
Even the handle went in behind the blade. The fat swallowed the blade, and Ehud left it there. The king’s bowels emptied.{k}
Ehud stepped out to the porch,{l} pulled the doors of the upstairs room closed, and locked them from outside.
After he left, the king’s servants came and saw the locked doors. “He must be using the toilet{m} in the cool inner room,” they said.
They waited so long they felt embarrassed. When the king still did not open the doors, they got a key and unlocked them. There on the floor lay their master, dead.
Ehud slipped away while they waited. He went past the carved stones and reached Seirah.
On arriving, he blew a ram’s horn in Ephraim’s hills. The Israelites came down from the hills with Ehud leading them.
“Come after me,” he said, “because Yahweh has put your enemy Moab in your power.” They went down behind him, took the Jordan crossings that led to Moab, and let nobody over.
At that time they killed about ten thousand Moabites, all of them strong, brave men. Not one got away.
That day Moab was crushed under Israel’s power. Eighty years of peace followed.
Next came Shamgar son of Anath.{n} With a stick used to drive oxen, six hundred Philistines fell to him. He, too, rescued Israel.

notes.text: Hebrew seren, a Philistine title, perhaps related to the Greek word tyrannos.
Or “the entrance of Hamath.”
The Asheroth were wooden poles or images linked to the goddess Asherah. The Greek Old Testament reads “the groves.”
Cushan-rishathaim means “Cushan of double wickedness,” probably a mocking twist on a foreign name.
That is, “Aram of the two rivers,” upper Mesopotamia.
Eglon sounds like the Hebrew word for “calf” (egel).
Ehud perhaps means “where is the glory?” The meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew “held back in his right hand.” The same phrase is used of the Benjaminite slingers in 20:16. Benjamin means “son of the right hand.”
Hebrew gomed, a measure found only here, perhaps a short cubit of about 13 inches (33 centimeters). The Greek Old Testament reads “a span” (about 9 inches, 23 centimeters).
Or “the stone quarries” (also in verse 26). The Hebrew word pesilim usually means carved idols.
The meaning of the rare Hebrew word parshedon is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament (B text) lacks this clause.
The meaning of the rare Hebrew word misderon is uncertain. It may mean “entrance hall” or “toilet room.”
Hebrew “covering his feet,” a polite way of speaking.
Anath was a Canaanite goddess of war. “Son of Anath” may point to Shamgar’s town (Beth-anath), or it may describe him as a warrior.

verses.text: Ehud was gone, and once more Israel did what Yahweh saw as evil.
So Yahweh gave them over to Jabin,{a} a Canaanite king whose throne was in Hazor. Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim,{b} commanded Jabin’s army.
Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots, and for twenty years he was cruel to the Israelites. At last they cried out to Yahweh for help.
At that time Israel’s judge was a prophet named Deborah,{c} the wife of Lappidoth.{d}
Her seat was under a palm tree named for her, Deborah’s Palm, in Ephraim’s hills between Ramah and Bethel. Israelites went up to her whenever they had a dispute.
She called Barak{e} son of Abinoam from Kedesh, a town of Naphtali. “Yahweh, Israel’s God, gives you this order,” she said. “Lead ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun up to Mount Tabor.
Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, will come to the Kishon Brook to fight you, with his chariots and his soldiers. I will give him into your power.”
Barak said to her, “If you will come with me, I will go. If you stay behind, so will I.”{f}
“I will certainly come,” she said. “But the honor in this trip will not go to you. Yahweh will let a woman defeat Sisera.” Then Deborah rose and went along with Barak to Kedesh.
Barak summoned the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali to meet in Kedesh. Ten thousand men went up behind him,{g} and Deborah went up too.
A man named Heber, a Kenite, had separated from the rest of the Kenites, who came from Hobab, Moses’ brother-in-law. Heber’s tent stood near Kedesh, beside the great tree at Zaanannim.{h}
Sisera heard that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor.
Sisera called out every chariot he had, nine hundred of them with iron fittings, and the troops who were with him. They moved from Harosheth-hagoyim toward the Kishon River.
“Go!” Deborah said to Barak. “This is the day Yahweh gives Sisera to you. Has Yahweh not gone out ahead of you?” So Barak hurried down from Mount Tabor, and ten thousand men followed.
Yahweh filled Sisera, his chariots, and his whole army with panic as Barak’s swords struck. Sisera jumped down from his chariot and ran away on foot.
Barak raced after the chariots and the soldiers as far as Harosheth-haggoyim. Sisera’s whole army fell by the sword. No one was left.
Sisera himself fled on foot to the tent of Jael,{i} who was married to Heber the Kenite. Peace stood between King Jabin of Hazor and Heber’s household.
Jael came out to greet Sisera. “Turn in here, my lord,” she said. “Turn in to me. Have no fear.” He entered her tent, and she hid him under a rug.
“Give me a little water to drink,” he said, “for I am thirsty.” She untied a leather bottle of milk, let him drink, and hid him again.
He said, “Stand in the doorway of the tent. If someone comes and asks whether a man is inside, tell him no.”

Then Jael, Heber’s wife, took a tent peg and picked up a hammer. Quietly she went to him as he lay in a deep sleep, worn out. She drove the peg through his head and pinned him to the ground. So he died.{j}

Barak arrived just then, still chasing Sisera. Jael stepped out to meet him. “Come,” she said, “and I will show you the man you want.” He followed her in, and there was Sisera on the ground, dead, the peg through his head.
So on that day God humbled Jabin, the Canaanite king, before Israel.
The Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin, king of Canaan, until they had wiped him out.

notes.text: Jabin means “he understands.” A king of Hazor with the same name appears in Joshua 11:1.
Harosheth-hagoyim perhaps means “woodland of the nations” or “farmland of the nations.”
Deborah means “bee.”
Or “a woman of fire” or “a fiery woman.” Lappidoth means “torches,” and it may be a name or a description.
Barak means “lightning.” Abinoam means “my father is pleasantness.”
The Greek Old Testament adds, “for I do not know the day on which the angel of Yahweh will give me success.”
Hebrew “at his feet,” that is, following him. The same phrase is used in verse 15 of chapter 5.

Or “the oak of Zaanannim.” The Greek Old Testament reads “the oak of the greedy ones.” Hobab is perhaps the same person as Jethro (Exodus 3:1) or a son of Reuel (Numbers 10:29). The Hebrew word for “father-in-law” can also mean “brother-in-law.”
Jael means “mountain goat.”
Or “he was fast asleep and worn out. So he died.” The Hebrew is hard to read. The Greek Old Testament reads “and he fainted away, and darkness fell on him, and he died.”

verses.text: On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song:

“When leaders let their hair hang loose{a} in Israel,
when the people give themselves freely,
praise Yahweh!

Hear this, you kings! Give ear, you rulers!
To Yahweh I will sing,
and to Israel’s God I will play my music.

“Yahweh, when you marched out of Seir,
when you walked from the fields of Edom,
the earth shook and the sky poured down rain.
Yes, the clouds poured down water.

“In the days of Shamgar son of Anath,
in the days of Jael,
the highways were empty.{d}
Travelers took the back paths.

Life in the villages{e} stopped.
It stopped in Israel
until I, Deborah, stood up,{f}
until I stood up as a mother for Israel.

New gods were what they picked,
and war pounded at their gates.{g}
Of forty thousand men in Israel,
not one carried shield or spear.

My heart is with Israel’s commanders,
who gave themselves freely among the people.
Praise Yahweh!

Listen to the singers{k} at the wells.
They tell of Yahweh’s victories,
the victories of his villagers in Israel.
Down to the gates Yahweh’s people marched.

“Awake, awake, Deborah!
Awake, awake, and start a song!
Rise up, Barak!
Lead your prisoners away, son of Abinoam.

Then a few survivors came down to the strong ones.
Yahweh’s people came down to join me against the mighty.{l}

Issachar’s princes were with Deborah.
Issachar was loyal to Barak
and rushed into the valley behind him.
In the clans of Reuben
there was long and serious thought.{o}

Why did you stay behind among the sheep pens,{p}
hearing the shepherds whistle to their flocks?
Among Reuben’s clans
there was much doubt.

Gilead stayed east of the Jordan.
And Dan, why did you hang around the ships?{q}
Asher sat still on the seacoast
and stayed by his harbors.

But Zebulun’s people risked their lives to the point of death,
and so did Naphtali, out on the high fields.

“Kings came and fought.
The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach,
by the waters of Megiddo.
They carried off no silver.

The stars fought from heaven.
Along their tracks in the sky
they fought Sisera.

Then the horses’ hooves pounded,
pounded as his strong horses galloped.

‘Put a curse on Meroz,’{t} said Yahweh’s messenger.
‘Put a bitter curse on those who live there,
for they did not come to help Yahweh,
to help Yahweh against the warriors.’

“Jael is the most blessed of women,
the wife of Heber the Kenite.
Of all women who live in tents, she is the most blessed.

He asked her for water, and milk was what she gave.
In a splendid bowl she brought him thick cream.

She reached her hand for the tent peg,
and her right hand for the hammer of a worker.
She struck Sisera and crushed his head.
She smashed his skull and pierced it through.

Between her feet he sank down and fell.
He lay still.
He sank down between her feet and fell.
And where he sank down, there he lay, dead.

“Sisera’s mother looked out the window.
She cried out from behind the lattice:
‘What is keeping his chariot?
Why are the wheels of his chariots so late?’

The wisest of her ladies answered her,
and she told herself the same thing:

‘They must be finding treasure and dividing it.
There must be a girl or two{u} for every man,
and colored cloth for Sisera,
colored cloth with fine stitching,
two pieces of stitched cloth
for the necks of those who took the loot.’{v}

“May all your enemies be destroyed like that, Yahweh!
But may those who love him shine like the rising sun in all its power.” After that, the land had rest for forty years.

notes.text: Or “When leaders take the lead.” The Hebrew phrase is one of many hard expressions in this ancient poem. It may mean that warriors let their hair hang loose to show they were dedicated (compare Numbers 6:5), or that leaders took charge. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “When a message was given in Israel.” Other Greek copies take it to mean rulers taking charge.
Or “flowed” or “melted.” The Hebrew may come from a word meaning “shake,” as the Greek Old Testament has it (“were shaken”), or from one meaning “flow.”
Or “this is Sinai,” or “even Sinai.” Many scholars take the Hebrew words zeh sinai as an ancient title, “the One of Sinai” (compare Psalm 68:8).
Or “caravans stopped.”

Or “Warriors.” The meaning of the Hebrew word perazon (also in verse 11) is not certain. It may mean people of villages without walls, or rulers or warriors. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “the mighty men.”
Or “until you stood up, Deborah, until you stood up.” The Hebrew form qamti can be read as an old form meaning “you.” The Greek Old Testament follows that reading (“until Deborah stood up”).

The Hebrew of this line is very hard. The Greek Old Testament (B text) agrees with “They had chosen new gods.” Some translators read “God chose new leaders.” The second part is also not certain (“then there was fighting in the gates,” or “then there was barley bread”).
Or “reddish-brown.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “at noon,” reading the Hebrew word as tsohorayim.
The meaning of the Hebrew word middin is not certain. It may mean “saddle blankets.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “on the judge’s seat,” linking it to the word for “judgment.”
Or “talk about it!” or “sing about it!”

Or “of those who divide the flocks,” or “of the musicians.” The meaning of the Hebrew word mechatsetsim is not certain. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “from the noise of troublemakers among the water carriers.”

The Hebrew of verse 13 is hard and has been read in several ways. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “Then those who remained went down to the strong. Yahweh’s people went down for him among the mighty ones from me.”
The meaning is not certain. Perhaps Ephraim had settled on land that Amalek once held. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “Ephraim pulled them up by the roots in Amalek.”
Or “the staff of the scribe,” or “the rod of the officer.” Hebrew shebet sopher.

Hebrew chiqqe-leb, “decisions of the heart.” Many Hebrew copies and the matching line in verse 16 read chiqre-leb, “searchings of the heart.” The difference is one letter. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “great pains reached the heart.”
Or “saddlebags” or “campfires.” The meaning of the Hebrew word mishpetayim is not certain.
Or “why did he live as a foreigner on ships?” The Hebrew verb gur means to stay as a foreign resident.
The meaning of the Hebrew word qedumim is not certain. It may mean “ancient,” or “rushing,” or “of battles.”
Or “You trampled the strong, O my soul!” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “my mighty soul will trample him down.”
The location of Meroz is not known.
Hebrew “a womb, two wombs,” a rough soldiers’ word for captive women.

The Hebrew of the last line is hard. Some read “for my neck as plunder,” or “for the neck of the queen.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) has “he will surely be kind to every man ... they are the spoils for his neck.”

verses.text: Once more the Israelites did what Yahweh saw as evil, and for seven years he let Midian rule over them.
Midian was too strong for Israel. Because of Midian, the Israelites dug themselves shelters in the hills, and they used caves and mountain forts.
Each time Israel planted crops, the people of Midian, Amalek, and the east marched in and attacked.
They pitched camp in the fields and destroyed the crops as far away as Gaza. Israel was left with no food at all. No sheep, ox, or donkey was spared.
They came with their herds and tents, swarming like locusts. No one could count the men or their camels. They poured into the land and wrecked it.
Midian left Israel starving, and the Israelites cried out to Yahweh.
The Israelites cried out to Yahweh about Midian,{a}
and Yahweh sent them a prophet. The prophet said, “This is the word of Yahweh, the God of Israel: ‘I led you up out of Egypt. I freed you from the place where you were slaves.
I saved you from the Egyptians and from everyone who beat you down. I pushed those people out ahead of you and gave you their land.
I told you, “I am Yahweh your God. Though you are living among Amorites, do not bow to their gods.” But you would not listen.’”
The messenger of Yahweh came and sat under the oak tree at Ophrah. It belonged to Joash, of the Abiezer family. His son Gideon{b} was beating out wheat in a winepress so that Midian would not see it.
The messenger of Yahweh appeared to Gideon and said, “Yahweh is with you, brave warrior.”

“But sir,” said Gideon, “if Yahweh is with us, why has all this come down on us? Where are the great wonders our parents told us of? They said, ‘Yahweh brought us up from Egypt.’ Yet now Yahweh has abandoned us and handed us to Midian.”
Yahweh faced him. “Go with all the strength you have,” he said, “and rescue Israel from Midian. Am I not the one sending you?”
Gideon replied, “Pardon me, Lord, but how could I save Israel? My clan is the smallest in Manasseh, and in my father’s house I am the youngest.”
Yahweh said to him, “I will be with you. You will beat Midian as if they were one man.”
Gideon said, “If you are pleased with me, give me a sign that you are really the one speaking to me.
Please do not leave until I bring you a gift and set it before you.” Yahweh said, “I will stay until you return.”

Gideon hurried in and cooked a young goat. He also baked flat bread without yeast from about three-fifths of a bushel{c} of flour. He placed the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot. Then he carried it all out to the oak and set it before him.
God’s messenger told him, “Lay the meat and the bread on that big rock, then pour the broth over all of it.” So Gideon did.
The messenger of Yahweh stretched out the staff in his hand and touched the meat and the bread with its tip. Fire jumped up from the rock and burned them up. Then the messenger of Yahweh was gone.
Then Gideon realized that this was Yahweh’s messenger. “Oh no, Lord Yahweh!” he cried. “I have looked right into the face of Yahweh’s messenger!”
But Yahweh told him, “Peace to you. Have no fear. You will not die.”
There Gideon built an altar to Yahweh and called it Yahweh Shalom.{d} It is still standing in Ophrah, the town of the Abiezer family.
That same night Yahweh told Gideon, “Take your father’s second bull, the seven-year-old.{e} Tear down your father’s altar to Baal, and cut down the Asherah pole{f} beside it.
Then build a proper altar to Yahweh your God on top of this hill fort. Take the second bull and burn it as an offering, using the wood of the Asherah pole you cut down.”
Gideon took ten of his servants and did just what Yahweh had said. He feared his family and the men of the town too much to act by day, so he did it by night.
The men of the town got up the next morning and found Baal’s altar torn down. The Asherah pole next to it was cut down, and the second bull lay burning on a new altar.
“Who has done this?” the men kept asking one another. They searched and questioned people until someone told them, “It was Gideon son of Joash.”
The men demanded of Joash, “Send your son out. He has to die! He broke Baal’s altar and chopped down the Asherah pole next to it.”

Joash answered the whole crowd pressing around him, “Are you going to fight for Baal? Are you going to rescue him? Anyone who fights for him will be dead by morning. If Baal is really a god, he can defend himself. Someone broke his altar!”
That day Gideon was given the name Jerubbaal,{g} meaning “Let Baal fight against him,” because he had torn down Baal’s altar.
Then all the Midianites, Amalekites, and eastern peoples joined together. Across the Jordan they came and made camp in the Jezreel Valley.
The Spirit of Yahweh came over Gideon like a coat.{h} He blew a ram’s horn, and the Abiezer family gathered to follow him.
He sent messengers all through Manasseh to call the men to arms. He also sent word to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and their men went up to meet them.
Gideon said to God, “You said you would save Israel through me.
So I am setting a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If dew falls on the fleece alone and the ground stays dry, then I will know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you said.”
And it happened that way. Early the next morning Gideon squeezed the fleece, and a full bowl of dew ran out of it.

Then Gideon said to God, “Please do not be angry with me. I will speak only this once more. One more test with the fleece, please. This time, let the fleece be dry and the ground around it covered with dew.”
That night God did it. Only the fleece was dry, and dew lay on all the ground around it.

notes.text: The Dead Sea Scroll 4QJudg-a, one of the oldest copies of Judges, does not have verses 7-10. Its text goes straight from verse 6 to verse 11. Many scholars think these verses, which are in the standard Hebrew text and the Greek Old Testament, were added later.
Gideon probably means “hacker” or “one who cuts down” (compare verses 25-32). Joash means “Yahweh has given.” Ophrah perhaps means “young deer.”
Hebrew “an ephah,” about 22 liters.
Yahweh Shalom means “Yahweh is peace.”

The Hebrew is hard to read. It may mean “your father’s young bull, and a second bull seven years old.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) agrees with the Hebrew: “the young bull ... even the second bull of seven years.”
A wooden pole or image linked to the goddess Asherah. It is also used in verses 26, 28, and 30.
Jerubbaal means “Let Baal fight.” In 2 Samuel 11:21 the name is changed to Jerubbesheth, with bosheth, “shame,” taking the place of Baal.
That is, he took hold of Gideon. Hebrew “put on Gideon like a garment.”

verses.text: At dawn Jerubbaal, also called Gideon, led his whole army to the spring of Harod.{a} Midian’s tents were pitched on the plain to the north, close to Moreh hill.{b}
Then Yahweh spoke to Gideon. “Your army is too large for me to give Midian to you. Israel would take the credit and say, ‘My own strength rescued me.’
So tell the soldiers, ‘If any of you is frightened and trembling, you may leave Mount Gilead and go home.’”{c} Twenty-two thousand left, and ten thousand remained.

Yahweh spoke again. “Still too many. Bring them to the stream, and I will sort them for you there. If I say about a man, ‘He will go along with you,’ then he goes. If I say, ‘He will not,’ then he does not.”
So Gideon led the men to the stream. There Yahweh told him, “Set apart those who lap with their tongues the way a dog does. Do the same with those who kneel down to drink.”
Three hundred scooped water to their mouths with their hands and lapped it.{d} The rest knelt and drank from the stream.
“The three hundred who lapped,” Yahweh told Gideon, “are the ones I will use to save you. Midian will fall into your power. Send everyone else home.”
The three hundred took over the food supplies and ram’s horns of the others. Gideon sent the rest of Israel’s men to their tents. Midian’s camp lay in the valley beneath him.
In the night Yahweh said to Gideon, “Rise and attack the camp. I am handing it to you.
But if you are afraid to attack, take your servant Purah and slip into the camp with him,
and hear what the Midianites are saying. Then you will have courage to strike.” So Gideon and Purah crept to the outer edge of the camp, where soldiers stood guard.
The Midianites, Amalekites, and eastern tribes covered the valley like a swarm of locusts. Nobody could count their camels. They were as many as the grains of sand by the sea.

Just as Gideon got close, one soldier was describing a dream to another. “I dreamed that a round barley loaf rolled into the Midianite camp,” he said. “It crashed into a tent and knocked it over. The tent lay flat.”
The other soldier answered, “That means the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has put Midian and its whole army in his hands.”
After Gideon heard about the dream and its meaning, he fell to the ground and worshiped. Back he went to the Israelite camp. “Up!” he called. “Yahweh has given Midian’s camp to you!”
Gideon split his three hundred men into three bands. He handed each man a ram’s horn and an empty jar. Inside every jar burned a torch.
“Keep your eyes on me,” he said, “and follow my lead. When I reach the edge of their camp, do exactly what I do.
I and those with me will sound our horns. Then you sound yours all around the camp and cry out, ‘For Yahweh and for Gideon!’”

It was the start of the middle watch (about ten at night){e} when Gideon and his hundred men reached the camp’s edge. The guards had just changed. Gideon’s men sounded their horns and shattered the jars they held.
The other two bands did the same, blowing horns and breaking jars. They gripped torches in their left hands and horns in their right. “A sword for Yahweh and for Gideon!” they shouted.
Each man stood still in his place around the camp. Inside, the soldiers ran in all directions, yelling as they fled.
As the three hundred horns kept blowing, Yahweh set every soldier’s sword against his own friend. The army fled as far as Beth-shittah, toward Zererah, and to the edge of Abel-meholah near Tabbath.
Then men from Naphtali, Asher, and all of Manasseh were summoned from Israel, and they ran after the Midianites.

Gideon also sent runners through Ephraim’s hills with this call: “Come down and fight Midian! Hold the crossings of the Jordan before they get there, all the way to Beth-barah.” Ephraim’s men all came and held the crossings as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan itself.

Two Midianite princes, Oreb and Zeeb,{f} were caught. Oreb died at a rock now called by his name, and Zeeb at a winepress called by his. The Israelites went on chasing Midian, and they carried the heads of Oreb and Zeeb over the Jordan to Gideon.

notes.text: Harod means “trembling” (compare verse 3).
Moreh means “teacher” or “one who gives oracles.”

Gilead is east of the Jordan, far from Gideon’s camp. Many scholars suspect an early copying mistake, perhaps for Mount Gilboa. Others take the Hebrew verb, found only here, to mean “and hurry away from Mount Gilead.”

In the Hebrew, the words “bringing water up in their hands to their mouths” stand in verse 6 with those who lapped, and the Greek Old Testament (B text) agrees. Some scholars think the words first belonged at the end of verse 5, with those who knelt.
Hebrew “the middle watch.” In the Old Testament the night was split into three watches: evening (until about 10 p.m.), middle (until about 2 a.m.), and morning (until about 6 a.m.).
Oreb means “raven,” and Zeeb means “wolf.”

subheads.9: The Dream of the Barley Loaf

verses.text: The men of Ephraim confronted Gideon. “Why did you do this to us?” they asked. “You never called us when you went to fight Midian!” They argued with him fiercely.
He answered them, “What have I done compared with you? The leftover grapes of Ephraim are better than the whole harvest of Abiezer.
God gave Oreb and Zeeb, the princes of Midian, into your hands. What was I able to do beside that?” When they heard this, their anger faded.
Gideon came to the Jordan and went across with the three hundred who were still with him. Weary as they were, they did not stop chasing the enemy.
He asked the people of Succoth{a} for help. “My men are exhausted,” he said. “Please hand them a few loaves. I am hunting Zebah and Zalmunna,{b} the Midianite kings.”
The leaders of Succoth answered, “Do you already hold Zebah and Zalmunna in your fist? Why should we feed your army?”
Gideon said, “Then this is what will happen. When Yahweh puts Zebah and Zalmunna in my power, I will beat{c} your bodies with desert thorns and briers.”
From Succoth he went up to Penuel{d} and asked them for the same help. The people of Penuel gave him the same answer as Succoth.
Then he warned the people of Penuel, “Once I return in peace, this tower of yours comes down.”

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, with an army of some fifteen thousand. These were all that were left of the armies of the eastern tribes. One hundred twenty thousand men with swords had already been killed.
Gideon went up by the desert road east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck the camp while the men there felt safe.
The two kings, Zebah and Zalmunna, fled, but Gideon ran them down. He seized both Midianite kings, and their whole army scattered in terror.
Afterward Gideon son of Joash came back from the battle by way of the Ascent of Heres.{e}
Gideon grabbed a young man of Succoth and quizzed him. The young man put in writing the names of the town’s officials and elders: seventy-seven men.
Gideon went to the men of Succoth. “Here they are, Zebah and Zalmunna!” he said. “You made fun of me. You said, ‘Are Zebah and Zalmunna already in your fist? Why should we feed your worn-out men?’”
He took the town’s elders, picked thorns and thistles in the desert, and taught the men of Succoth a painful lesson with them.{f}
He also pulled down the tower of Penuel and put the men of that town to death.
Gideon then turned to Zebah and Zalmunna. “Describe the men you killed at Tabor,” he said. They answered, “They were like you. Each one had the look of a prince.”
“Those men were my brothers,” Gideon said, “sons of my own mother. By the life of Yahweh, I would not be killing you today if you had left them alive.”
Gideon told Jether, his oldest son, “Get up and kill them!” The boy did not draw his sword. He was only a boy, and he was scared.
Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Do it yourself! A man is as strong as his years.” So Gideon got up and killed them. He took the moon-shaped ornaments that hung on their camels’ necks.
The people of Israel urged Gideon, “Become our ruler. Let your son rule after you, and his son after him. You are the one who set us free from Midian.”
Gideon told them, “I will not rule you, and neither will my son. Yahweh is the one who will rule you.”
Then Gideon said, “There is one thing I ask. Every one of you, give me an earring from what you took in the battle.” (Those enemy soldiers wore gold earrings, as Ishmaelites did.{g})
“We will gladly give them,” they said. They spread out a cloak, and every man tossed onto it the earrings he had taken.

The earrings he asked for added up to about forty-three pounds of gold.{h} That did not include the moon-shaped ornaments, the pendants, or the purple robes of Midian’s kings, or the chains from the camels’ necks.
Gideon made the gold into an ephod{i} and put it in Ophrah, his own town. All Israel went after it there like a faithless wife. It snared Gideon and his household.
That is how Midian was brought low before Israel. They never held up their heads again. In Gideon’s time the land was at rest for forty years.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went home and lived there.
Seventy sons were born to Gideon,{j} because he had a good many wives.
A slave woman of his in Shechem also gave him a son, and Gideon named him Abimelech.{k}
Gideon son of Joash lived to a ripe old age and then died. His body was laid in the grave of his father Joash, in Ophrah, where the Abiezer family lived.
Gideon was hardly in his grave when the Israelites again ran after the Baals like unfaithful wives. They made Baal-berith{l} their god.
They forgot Yahweh their God, who had saved them from all the enemies around them.
They were not loyal to the family of Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, either, though he had done so much good for Israel.

notes.text: Succoth means “booths” or “shelters.”
Zebah means “sacrifice,” and Zalmunna perhaps means “protection withheld.” The names may be twisted on purpose from the kings’ real names.
Or “tear.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “tear your flesh with the thorns of the desert and the Barkenim,” keeping the Hebrew word for “briers” as a name.
Penuel means “face of God” (Genesis 32:30).
Or “from the battle before sunrise.” Heres means “sun.”
Hebrew “made to know.” Many scholars read “threshed” (compare verse 7), which is a small difference in the Hebrew letters. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “tore.”
Here the word means desert traders in general. Compare Genesis 37:25-28, where Ishmaelites and Midianites are named together.
Hebrew “1,700 shekels,” about 43 pounds.
An ephod was a priest’s garment (Exodus 28:6-14). Here it seems to be an object used in worship or for asking God for answers.
Hebrew “who came out of his thigh.”
Abimelech means “my father is king.”
Baal-berith means “lord of the covenant.” Compare El-berith in 9:46.

verses.text: Abimelech, a son of Jerubbaal, went to Shechem to see his mother’s brothers. He spoke to them and to his mother’s whole clan.
“Put this question to every leader in Shechem,{a}” he said. “Which is better for you: seventy rulers, the sons of Jerubbaal, or one ruler? And do not forget that I am from your own bones and blood.”
His mother’s brothers carried this message to every leader in Shechem. The leaders leaned toward Abimelech, for they said, “He is our relative.”
The leaders handed him seventy pieces of silver{b} from the temple of Baal-berith. With it Abimelech paid a gang of worthless, reckless men, and they became his followers.

Abimelech then traveled to Ophrah, to the house of his father. On a single stone he killed his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal. Jotham,{c} the youngest, was the only one who lived, since he had hidden.
Then all the leaders of Shechem and of Beth-millo{d} met at the oak by the stone pillar{e} in Shechem and made Abimelech their king.
When news of this reached Jotham, he went up and stood on Mount Gerizim’s peak. He called out in a loud voice: “Hear me, you leaders of Shechem, and may God hear you in return!
Once the trees went out to pick a king. To the olive tree they said, ‘Rule over us.’
But the olive tree said, ‘Am I to give up the rich oil that brings honor to gods and to people, and go sway over the trees?’
Then the trees approached the fig tree. ‘You come,’ they said, ‘and rule over us.’
The fig tree said, ‘Am I to give up my sweetness and my good fruit, and go off to wave above the trees?’
Then the trees turned to the grapevine. ‘You come,’ they said, ‘and rule over us.’
But the vine said, ‘Am I to give up the new wine that makes gods and people glad, and go sway over the trees?’
In the end every tree called to the thornbush, ‘You come and rule over us.’
The thornbush answered them, ‘If you are truly anointing me as your king, come and shelter under my shade. If you are not, then flames will shoot from the thornbush and burn the cedars of Lebanon.’
“Now ask yourselves whether you acted with honesty and good faith when you crowned Abimelech. Did you treat Jerubbaal and his house justly? Did you reward him for what he did?
My father fought on your side. He gambled his own life to rescue you from the power of Midian.

But now you have attacked my father’s house. Seventy of his sons died on a single stone at your hands. You crowned Abimelech, his slave woman’s son, ruler of Shechem’s leaders, simply because he is your kinsman.
If today you have been honest and fair to Jerubbaal and his family, then enjoy Abimelech, and may he enjoy you.
Otherwise, let fire blaze out of Abimelech and eat up Shechem’s leaders and Beth-millo. Let fire also blaze out of Shechem’s leaders and Beth-millo and eat up Abimelech!”
After saying this, Jotham ran off and escaped to Beer.{f} Fear of his brother Abimelech kept him living there.
For three years Abimelech held power over Israel.
Then God stirred up bad feelings between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and they betrayed Abimelech.

God did this so that the wrong done to Jerubbaal’s seventy sons would come back on the guilty. Their blood was put on their brother Abimelech, their killer, and on the leaders of Shechem who had strengthened his hands to kill them.
The leaders of Shechem set men to wait in ambush for Abimelech on the mountaintops. These men robbed everyone who passed that way, and Abimelech was told.
Gaal son of Ebed{g} moved into Shechem with his brothers, and the leaders of the town put their trust in him.

They went out to the fields, gathered grapes from their vineyards, and trampled them. Then they held a festival.{h} They went into their god’s temple, and there they feasted, got drunk, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech? Who is Shechem, that we should be his servants? He is only Jerubbaal’s son, and Zebul is his officer. Serve the descendants of Hamor, the father of Shechem! Why should we serve Abimelech?
“If only these people were mine to command,” he said, “I would soon remove Abimelech.” Then he called out this challenge to Abimelech:{i} “Bring out your whole army and fight!”
When Zebul, the town’s ruler, heard what Gaal son of Ebed was saying, his anger blazed.
Zebul sent men to Abimelech with a secret message.{j} “Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have arrived in Shechem,” it said. “They are turning the whole town against you.
Tonight you and your men should get up and wait in ambush in the fields.
In the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rush at the town. Gaal and his men will come out to face you, and you can do to them whatever you find best.”
So Abimelech and all his men rose in the night and set an ambush above Shechem. They split into four groups.
Gaal son of Ebed went out and took his stand in the doorway of the town gate. Abimelech and his men rose from their hiding places.
When Gaal caught sight of them, he said to Zebul, “Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!” Zebul answered, “Those are the shadows on the hills. They only look like men to you.”
But Gaal spoke again. “Look, men are coming down from the middle of the land,{k} and one group is coming from the road to the Diviners’ Oak.”{l}
Zebul said, “So where is that big mouth of yours? You said, ‘Who is Abimelech? Why should we serve him?’ Here are the men you made fun of. Go out and fight!”
Gaal marched out in front of the leaders of Shechem and attacked Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and Gaal fled. Many of his men fell wounded along the road, right up to the gate.
Abimelech stayed at Arumah. Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem so they could not live there.
Next day the Shechem people went out to work in the fields, and word of it reached Abimelech.
He divided his men into three bands and placed them in ambush in the fields. When the people came out of the town, he leaped out and struck them down.
Abimelech and his group rushed ahead and took their place at the town gate. The other two groups ran at the people in the fields and cut them down.
Abimelech fought against the town the whole day. He took it and killed the people inside. Then he leveled the town and spread salt on the ground.
Hearing this news, the leaders in the Tower of Shechem hid in the inner room{m} of the temple of El-berith.{n}
News came to Abimelech that all of those leaders were crowded together there.
He climbed Mount Zalmon{o} with all his men. Abimelech picked up an axe, chopped a branch from a tree, and hoisted it onto his shoulder. He told his men, “Hurry! Do just what you have seen me do.”

Every one of them cut a branch and followed Abimelech. They piled the branches against the inner room and set fire to it over the people inside. So the whole Tower of Shechem burned, and about a thousand men and women died.
Abimelech moved on to Thebez, surrounded it, and took it.
In the center of the town stood a strong tower. Every man and woman in the town, including its leaders, ran there, locked themselves in, and went up on the roof.
Abimelech came up to the tower and attacked it. He went close to its door to set it on fire.
Then a woman dropped the top stone of a millstone on his head, and it cracked his skull.
Abimelech shouted at his armor bearer, “Take your sword and finish me off, so no one will ever say a woman killed me.” The servant stabbed him, and Abimelech died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home.
In this way God gave Abimelech what he deserved for the wrong he did to his father by killing seventy brothers.
God also made the men of Shechem pay for every wicked deed. Jotham son of Jerubbaal had cursed them, and the curse came true.

notes.text: Or “citizens” or “lords.” The Hebrew word is ba’ale, a plural of baal, “owner, lord.” It is used this way all through the chapter.
Hebrew “seventy of silver,” probably shekels, which would weigh about 1 3/4 pounds.
Jotham means “Yahweh is perfect.”
Beth-millo means “house of the fill.” It was probably a fort built on a platform of earth.
Hebrew elon mutstsab. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “by the oak of the station” and adds a second reading of the same Hebrew word (“of the finder”). The A text does not have the addition.
Beer means “well.”
Gaal perhaps means “hatred,” and Ebed means “servant” or “slave.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “Gaal son of Jobel.”
Hebrew hillulim, a festival of praise held at the grape harvest. The Greek Old Testament (B text) keeps the Hebrew word (“made ellulim”). The A text reads “made dances.”
This follows the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament reads “I would say to Abimelech.”
Or “at Tormah.” The meaning of the Hebrew word betormah, found only here, is not certain. Some read “at Arumah” (verse 41).
Hebrew “the navel of the land.”
Hebrew elon me’onenim. The Greek Old Testament (B text) keeps the Hebrew words as a name. The A text translates them: “the way of the oak of the seers.”
Or “inner room.” The meaning of the Hebrew word tseriach is not certain. It is also used in verse 49.
El-berith means “God of the covenant.” Compare Baal-berith in 8:33 and 9:4.
Zalmon means “dark” or “shady.”

verses.text: After Abimelech’s time, Tola rose up to rescue Israel. He belonged to Issachar, and his family line ran back through Puah to Dodo. Tola made his home in Shamir, in the hills of Ephraim.
Tola led Israel twenty-three years. At his death he was buried in Shamir.
Jair from Gilead came next. He led Israel for twenty-two years.
Jair had thirty sons, and they rode thirty donkeys. They also owned thirty towns,{a} which are still called Havvoth-jair{b} today. They lie in the land of Gilead.
Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

Again the Israelites did what was evil in Yahweh’s eyes. They served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. They served the gods of Aram, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines. They turned away from Yahweh and stopped serving him.
Yahweh’s anger flared up against Israel. He gave them over to the Philistines and to the Ammonites.
That year the Ammonites beat down and crushed the Israelites. For eighteen years they bullied all the Israelites living east of the Jordan, in Gilead, the land of the Amorites.
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and the family of Ephraim. Israel was in deep trouble.
The Israelites cried out to Yahweh. “We have sinned against you,” they said. “We left our God and served the Baals.”
Yahweh answered them, “Think back. Did I not save you from Egypt? From the Amorites? From the Ammonites? From the Philistines?
When the Sidonians, the Amalekites, and the Maonites{c} pushed you around, you cried to me, and I saved you from them.
Still, you walked away from me and served other gods. This time I will not rescue you.
Go and cry out to the gods you chose! Let them be the ones to save you in your hour of trouble.”
The Israelites begged Yahweh, “We have sinned. Do whatever you think is right with us. Just save us today, please.”
Then they threw away the foreign gods they had among them and served Yahweh. And Yahweh could not stand to see Israel suffer any longer.{d}
The Ammonites were called up for war and camped in Gilead. Meanwhile the Israelites gathered at Mizpah and set up their own camp.
The leaders of Gilead asked each other, “Who will be the first to attack the Ammonites? That man will become the chief of everyone living in Gilead.”

notes.text: The Hebrew plays with words here. The word ‘ayarim means both “donkeys” and “towns.”
Havvoth-jair means “villages of Jair” (compare Numbers 32:41).
The Greek Old Testament reads “Midian.”
Hebrew “his soul was short with the misery of Israel,” that is, he lost patience with their suffering.

verses.text: Jephthah{a} from Gilead was a mighty warrior. His mother was a prostitute, and his father was Gilead.
Gilead’s wife had sons of her own. When they were grown, they forced Jephthah to leave. “You will get nothing from our father’s family,” they told him. “Your mother was another woman.”
Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Worthless men joined him there and went out on raids with him.
Some time later the Ammonites made war on Israel.
As the fighting with Ammon began, the elders of Gilead set out to fetch Jephthah home from Tob.
“Come and lead our army,” they said, “so that we can fight the Ammonites.”
Jephthah answered the elders of Gilead, “You hated me. You threw me out of my father’s house. Is it only trouble that brings you to me now?”
The elders said, “That is the very reason we have come back to you. Go with us and fight the Ammonites. Then you will be the ruler of all who live in Gilead.”
Jephthah asked them, “Suppose you bring me back to fight the Ammonites, and Yahweh gives them to me. Will I really be your ruler?”
The elders replied, “May Yahweh be our witness. We will do just what you say.”
So Jephthah left with the elders of Gilead. The people appointed him as their ruler and army leader. Then at Mizpah, Jephthah repeated all that he had said in front of Yahweh.
Jephthah sent men with a message for the king of Ammon. “What have you got against me?” they asked. “Why do you march into my land?”
The king of Ammon told Jephthah’s messengers, “When Israel came up out of Egypt, they took my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. Now give it back, and let us have peace.”
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of Ammon a second time.
“Jephthah says this,” they told him. “Israel did not take any land from Moab or from Ammon.
After leaving Egypt, they crossed the desert to the Red Sea{b} and came to Kadesh.

From there Israel sent word to the king of Edom: ‘Please let us go through your land.’ But the king of Edom would not hear of it. The king of Moab got the same request, and he too said no. So Israel stayed on at Kadesh.
Then they went around Edom and Moab through the desert. They came to the east side of Moab and camped on the far side of the Arnon. They never entered Moab, because the Arnon was Moab’s border.
Israel then sent word to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who ruled from Heshbon. ‘Allow us to cross your land on our way home,’ they said.
But Sihon did not trust Israel enough to let them cross his land. He called out his whole army, camped at Jahaz, and fought Israel.
Yahweh, the God of Israel, put Sihon and all his army in Israel’s hands, and Israel defeated them. So all the land of the Amorites in that country became Israel’s.
Israel took the whole Amorite territory. It stretched from the Arnon on one side to the Jabbok on the other, and from the desert to the Jordan.
Yahweh, the God of Israel, cleared the Amorites away so that his people could have room. Do you now think you can take it from us?
Do you not hold on to whatever Chemosh, your god, gives you? We will hold on to everything Yahweh our God has given us.
Are you a better king than Balak son of Zippor, who ruled Moab? Did that man ever pick a fight with Israel?
For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, the villages around them, and all the towns along the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during all that time?
I have done nothing wrong to you, yet you are doing wrong to me by going to war with me. May Yahweh, the Judge, rule today between Israel and Ammon.”
But the Ammonite king would not listen to Jephthah’s message.
Then Yahweh’s Spirit filled Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah he marched against the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to Yahweh. “If you really put the Ammonites in my power,” he said,
“then the first living thing{c} that comes through the door of my house to meet me, when I come home safe from Ammon, will belong to Yahweh. I will burn it as an offering to him.”
Jephthah went over to fight the Ammonites, and Yahweh gave them to him.
He struck them down with a great slaughter, from Aroer to near Minnith, taking twenty towns, and as far as Abel-keramim.{d} So the Ammonites were beaten down by Israel.
When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, his daughter came out to meet him, dancing and beating a tambourine. She was his only child. Besides her he had neither son nor daughter.
As soon as he saw her, he ripped his clothes. “Oh, my daughter!” he cried. “You have broken my heart. You have become a cause of my pain. I gave Yahweh my word, and I cannot take it back.”
She said, “Father, you gave Yahweh your word. Do to me what you promised, now that Yahweh has punished your enemies, the Ammonites.”
Then she said, “Let me ask for one thing. Give me two months to go and wander{e} in the hills with my friends and cry because I will never marry.”
“Go,” he said, and two months were hers. She and her friends climbed into the hills and cried for her lost chance to marry.
When the two months were over, she came back to her father, and he kept the promise he had made. She never slept with a man.{f} This led to a custom in Israel.
Each year Israel’s young women spent four days remembering{g} Jephthah’s daughter from Gilead.

notes.text: Jephthah means “he opens” or “he sets free.”
Hebrew yam suf, which means “Sea of Reeds.”
Or “whoever.” The Hebrew can mean a person or an animal. Houses in those days often kept animals on the ground floor.
Abel-keramim means “meadow of vineyards.”
Hebrew “go down.” Many scholars change one small thing in the Hebrew and read “wander.”

Some readers, ancient and modern, understand verses 39-40 to mean that Jephthah set his daughter apart to stay unmarried for life, not that he offered her as a sacrifice. The plain meaning of verse 31 is a burnt offering.
Or “to cry for” or “to tell the story of.” The meaning of the Hebrew verb is not certain.

verses.text: The men of Ephraim called out their army and crossed to Zaphon.{a} They said to Jephthah, “You went to fight the Ammonites and never called us to go with you. Why? We will set your house on fire with you inside!”
Jephthah answered, “My people and I were in a hard fight with Ammon. I called you for help, but you did not save me from them.
When I saw that you would not help, I put my life in danger and crossed over against the Ammonites. Yahweh gave them to me. So why come up here today to fight me?”

Jephthah then gathered all the men of Gilead and fought Ephraim. The Gileadites won, because Ephraim had mocked them: “You people of Gilead ran away from Ephraim. You live between Ephraim and Manasseh.”{b}

The Gileadites seized the crossings of the Jordan to cut off Ephraim. When an Ephraimite who had escaped said, “Let me cross,” the men of Gilead asked, “Do you belong to Ephraim?” If he answered, “No,”

they said, “Then say ‘Shibboleth.’”{c} If he said “Sibboleth,” because he could not say the word right, they grabbed him and killed him at the Jordan crossing. Ephraim lost forty-two thousand{d} men in this way.
Jephthah led Israel six years. Then Jephthah of Gilead died, and he was buried in a town of Gilead.{e}
After him Ibzan from Bethlehem{f} led Israel.
Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters to husbands outside the clan and brought home thirty brides from outside for his sons. His time as leader lasted seven years.
Ibzan died, and Bethlehem was where they buried him.
Elon from the tribe of Zebulun led Israel after him, for ten years.
Elon of Zebulun died and was buried in Aijalon, in Zebulun’s land.
Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, led Israel after him.
Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons. They rode seventy donkeys. He led Israel for eight years.
Abdon son of Hillel from Pirathon died and was buried in Pirathon, in Ephraim’s land, in the hills of the Amalekites.

notes.text: Or “northward.” Zaphon was a town in the Jordan Valley (Joshua 13:27).

The meaning of the Ephraimites’ mocking words is not certain. The Greek Old Testament (B text) says that the Ephraimites who got away were the ones speaking: “You are of Gilead in the midst of Ephraim and in the midst of Manasseh.”

Hebrew shibboleth means “head of grain” or “flowing stream.” The Ephraimites’ way of talking seems to have lacked the “sh” sound, so they said “sibboleth” with an “s.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) translates the word as “head of grain” (Stachys). The A text translates it as “password.”
Or “forty-two units.” On the Hebrew word elef (“thousand,” and perhaps also “clan” or “military unit”), compare 20:2.
Hebrew “in the towns of Gilead.” The Greek Old Testament reads “in his town, in Gilead.”
This was probably the Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15), not Bethlehem of Judah.

verses.text: Once more the Israelites did what Yahweh saw as evil, and he gave them to the Philistines for forty years.
In Zorah lived a man of the Dan family named Manoah.{a} His wife could not have children.
Yahweh’s messenger appeared to her with a word: “Up to now you have had no children, for you could not. Yet a son is coming, and you will carry him.
Take care, then. Strong drink and wine are not for you, and neither is any food that is unclean.
You are expecting a son. No razor may ever touch his head, for he will be set apart to God as a Nazirite{b} from the day he is born. He will start the work of freeing Israel from the Philistines.”

She hurried to her husband. “A man of God visited me,” she said. “His face was like the face of God’s own messenger, and it filled me with fear. I never asked where he lived, and he never gave me his name.

He did say this: ‘A son is coming, and you will carry him. From today, keep away from wine and strong drink, and from unclean food. The boy is set apart to God as a Nazirite for his whole life, to the day he dies.’”
Manoah prayed to Yahweh. “Lord, I beg you, send that man of God back to us. Let him teach us what to do when the boy is born and growing up.”
God answered Manoah. His messenger returned to the woman as she sat in the field, but her husband Manoah was not there.
She ran off to tell him. “Come!” she said. “The man who visited me before is here again.”
Manoah rose and went after his wife. Reaching the man, he asked, “Are you the one who talked with my wife?” “Yes,” he said.
Manoah asked, “When all this happens, how are we to raise the boy? What is he to do with his life?”
Yahweh’s messenger replied, “Your wife must keep everything I told her.
Nothing from the grapevine is for her. No wine, no strong drink, and no unclean food. She must follow every order I gave her.”
Manoah said to Yahweh’s messenger, “Stay with us, please. We will get a young goat ready for you.”

Yahweh’s messenger answered, “Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But a burnt offering, if you wish to make one, should go to Yahweh.” (Manoah had not yet realized that this was Yahweh’s messenger.)
Manoah said, “Tell us your name. Then, when it all comes true, we can honor you.”
Yahweh’s messenger said, “Why ask for my name? No one could grasp it.”{c}
Manoah took a young goat and a grain offering and laid them on a rock as an offering to Yahweh. As Manoah and his wife watched, Yahweh did something amazing.{d}
The flame rose from the altar toward the sky, and Yahweh’s messenger rose with it. Manoah and his wife saw it and dropped to the ground, faces down.
Yahweh’s messenger never showed himself to Manoah and his wife again. Only then did Manoah realize who he had been.
“We are going to die,” Manoah told his wife. “We have seen God.”
But she answered, “If Yahweh had meant to put us to death, would he have taken our burnt offering and grain offering? Would he have let us see all this, or told us what he did today?”
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson.{e} The boy grew, and Yahweh blessed him.
The Spirit of Yahweh began to stir in him at Mahaneh-dan,{f} between Zorah and Eshtaol.

notes.text: Manoah means “rest.”
Nazirite means “one set apart” (see Numbers 6:1-21). The Greek Old Testament (B text) keeps the Hebrew word (Nazir). The A text reads Naziraios, a form close to the wording of Matthew 2:23.
Hebrew pil’i, “wonderful, beyond understanding.” Compare Isaiah 9:6.
Hebrew “and he did wonderfully,” meaning the messenger. The Greek Old Testament (A text) reads “offered it to Yahweh, who does wonders.”
Samson (Hebrew Shimshon) is related to shemesh, “sun.” It may mean “little sun” or “of the sun.” Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun,” was near Zorah.
Mahaneh-dan means “camp of Dan” (compare 18:12).

verses.text: Samson went down to Timnah, and there he saw a young Philistine woman.
When he came back, he said to his parents, “In Timnah I saw a Philistine woman. Get her for me as my wife.”

His parents said, “Surely some woman from our own relatives or our own people would do. Why go to the Philistines, who do not know our God, for a wife?” But Samson told his father, “Get her. She is the one I want.”
His parents did not know that Yahweh was behind this. He wanted a chance to confront the Philistines, who were ruling Israel then.
Samson went down to Timnah with his parents. As they came near the vineyards there, a young lion roared and ran at him.
The Spirit of Yahweh rushed on him with power. Samson ripped the lion apart with nothing but his hands, as if it were a young goat. Yet he said nothing to his parents about it.
After that, he went down and spoke to the woman, and she pleased him.
Later he set out again to marry her. On the way he turned aside to look at the dead lion. A swarm of bees had settled in its body, and there was honey in it.
He scooped some into his hands and ate it as he walked along. He gave some to his parents when he reached them, and they ate it too. But he did not say that the honey came from the body of a lion.
His father went down to see the woman, and Samson gave a feast there, as young men did in those days.
When the people saw him,{a} they chose thirty young men to keep him company.
Samson said to them, “Here is a riddle for you. Work it out before the seven days of the feast are over, and I will give you thirty linen shirts and thirty sets of fine clothes.
If you cannot, then you must give me thirty linen shirts and thirty changes of fine clothes.” “Tell us your riddle,” they said. “We are listening.”
He said, “From the one who eats came food. From the strong one came something sweet.” Three days went by, and they could not work it out.

On the seventh day{b} they went to Samson’s wife. “Persuade your husband to give us the answer,” they said. “If you will not, we will set fire to you and your father’s house. Did you ask us here to strip us of everything we own?”

Samson’s wife threw herself on him, weeping. “You hate me!” she said. “You do not love me at all. You set my people a riddle, but you have not told me what it means.” “Not even my own father and mother know it,” he said. “Why should I tell you?”
She cried on him for the whole seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he gave in, because she kept pressing him. Then she told her people the answer.

Just before the sun set on the seventh day,{c} the townsmen came to him. “What is sweeter than honey?” they asked. “What is stronger than a lion?” Samson said, “If you had not used my young cow to plow, you would never have solved my riddle.”

Then the Spirit of Yahweh rushed on him with power. He went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty of its men. He stripped them of their clothes and handed these to the men who had answered the riddle. Then, burning with anger, he went back to his father’s house.
Samson’s wife was given to the friend who had stood beside him at the wedding.

notes.text: This follows the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament. With other vowels, the Hebrew could be read “Because they feared him.”
This follows the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament and some other old translations read “the fourth day,” which fits better with verses 14 and 17.
Hebrew harsah, “toward the sun” (a rare word for the sun). Many scholars change one letter and read “before he went into the bridal room.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “before sunrise.”

verses.text: Some time later, during the wheat harvest (May or June),{a} Samson visited his wife and brought her a young goat. “I want to go to my wife in her room,” he said. But her father would not allow it.
Her father said, “I was certain you hated her, so she is now the wife of your best man. Look, her younger sister is lovelier. Have her instead.”
Samson said to them, “This time no one can blame me for what I do to the Philistines.”
Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes.{b} He tied them tail to tail in pairs and fixed a torch between each two tails.
He set fire to the torches and sent the foxes into the Philistines’ ripe grain. Stacked grain, standing grain, vineyards, and olive trees all went up in flames.

The Philistines asked, “Who did this?” Someone answered, “Samson. His wife’s father, the man of Timnah, took her away and gave her to Samson’s friend.” Then the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
Samson told them, “Since you have done this, I swear I will pay you back. Then I will stop.”
He attacked them with fury and killed many.{c} Then he left and settled in a cave inside the rock of Etam.
The Philistines marched up into Judah and made camp. They spread out near Lehi.{d}
The men of Judah asked, “What do you want with us? Why have you come to fight?” The Philistines said, “We have come for Samson. We want to tie him up and give him the same treatment he gave us.”

So three thousand men of Judah went down to Samson’s cave in the rock of Etam. “Have you forgotten that the Philistines are our rulers?” they said. “Look what you have brought on us!” He said, “I only did to them what they did to me.”
They said, “We are here to tie you up and deliver you to the Philistines.” Samson said, “Then promise me you will not kill me yourselves.”
“No,” they said. “All we will do is tie you and turn you over to them. We swear we will not kill you.” They bound him with two new ropes and brought him up out of the rock.
As he neared Lehi, the Philistines came running at him, shouting. The Spirit of Yahweh rushed on him with power. The ropes around his arms turned to charred threads and dropped from his wrists.
Nearby lay the jawbone of a donkey, still fresh. He grabbed it and used it to strike down a thousand men.
“With a donkey’s jawbone I made one heap, then two,”{e} Samson said. “With that same jawbone I cut down a thousand men.”
When he was done speaking, he tossed the jawbone aside. The place got the name Ramath-lehi.{f}
Samson grew terribly thirsty. He called to Yahweh, “You gave your servant this great win. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of men who do not know you?”
God broke open a hollow in the ground at Lehi, and water flowed out. Samson drank, and his strength came back to him. That is why the spring is called En-hakkore.{g} It can still be seen at Lehi.
Samson led Israel twenty years, during the time when the Philistines ruled.

notes.text: The wheat harvest came after the barley harvest, in late spring. It fell roughly in the Hebrew month Sivan (the time of Pentecost, also called Shavuot), in May or June.
Or “jackals.”
Hebrew “leg upon thigh,” a saying for a crushing defeat.
Lehi means “jawbone.”
Hebrew hamor homoratayim, a play on words. Hamor means “donkey,” and homer means “heap.” The Greek Old Testament reads “I have completely destroyed them.”
Ramath-lehi means “height of the jawbone.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) understands it as “the lifting (or throwing away) of the jawbone.”
En-hakkore means “spring of the one who called.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “Well of the one who prayed.”

verses.text: Samson once traveled to Gaza. He noticed a prostitute there and stayed the night in her house.
Word spread through Gaza: “Samson has come here!” The men surrounded the place and lay in wait for him all night at the town gate. They kept still, telling each other, “At daybreak we will kill him.”

But Samson lay there only until midnight. Then he got up, seized the town gate by its doors, and tore the whole thing out, posts and bar together. He hoisted the doors onto his shoulders and hauled them to the crest of the hill facing Hebron.
Later, Samson fell for a woman in the Valley of Sorek.{a} Delilah{b} was her name.

The Philistine rulers visited her. “Coax him,” they said. “Learn the reason for his great strength, and find a way to overpower him and bind him so he cannot fight. We will each give you a payment of eleven hundred pieces of silver.”{c}
Delilah began, “Samson, tell me where your great strength comes from. What would it take to tie you up and leave you helpless?”
Samson answered, “Tie me with seven new bowstrings{d} that are still wet. Then I will lose my strength and be like any man.”
The Philistine rulers carried seven new, damp bowstrings to Delilah, and she tied Samson up with them.
Men were hidden in the inner room. She called out, “Samson! The Philistines are coming for you!” He snapped the strings like a strand of flax that breaks in a flame. His secret was still safe.
Delilah told Samson, “You have made a fool of me and lied to me. Now be honest. What would it take to tie you up?”
He said, “Tie me tight with ropes that are new and unused. Then my strength will go, and I will be like anyone else.”
Delilah found new ropes and bound him. “Samson!” she called. “The Philistines are coming for you!” Men were hiding in the inner room. He snapped the ropes off his arms as easily as a cobweb.
Delilah said, “All this time you have been joking and lying to me. Tell me how to tie you.” He said, “Take the seven braids of my hair and weave them into a cloth on the loom.”{e}
She fastened it down with a peg and called, “Samson! The Philistines are coming for you!” He woke from his sleep and tore away the peg, the loom, and the cloth.
She said, “You tell me you love me, but you hide your heart from me. Three times you have laughed at me. You still have not said where your great strength comes from.”
Every day she pestered him with her words, until he was sick to death of it.

At last he told her all that was in his heart. “A razor has never touched my head,” he said. “God set me apart as a Nazirite from birth. Shave my head and my strength will leave me. I will be as weak as everyone else.”
Delilah knew he had finally told her everything. She sent for the Philistine rulers: “Come one more time. He has opened his heart to me.” The rulers came, carrying the silver.
While Samson slept with his head resting on her knees, Delilah called a man, who cut off the seven braids of his hair. She began to weaken him,{f} and his strength left him.
“Samson!” she called. “The Philistines are coming for you!” He woke and thought, “I will shake myself free, as I always have.” He had no idea Yahweh had left him.
The Philistines grabbed him and dug out his eyes. They brought him down to Gaza, fastened him with bronze chains, and made him turn the grinding stone in the prison.
Yet his hair began to grow back after it was shaved.
The Philistine rulers met to hold a great feast, with a sacrifice to Dagon,{g} their god. They were full of joy. “Our god has given Samson, our enemy, into our power!” they said.
When the crowd saw him, they sang praises to their god. “Our god has put the man who destroyed our land into our power,” they said. “He killed so many of us!”
As the party grew merry, they shouted, “Call Samson, and let him put on a show!” So Samson was fetched from the prison, and he performed for them. They stood him between the pillars.
Samson said to the boy who held his hand, “Guide me to the pillars that hold up this building. I want to lean against them.”
