The building was packed wall to wall. Every Philistine ruler was inside. On the roof stood about three thousand more men and women, watching as Samson was made to perform.
Then Samson called to Yahweh, “Lord Yahweh, remember me! God, give me strength one more time. With one blow let me pay the Philistines back for my two eyes.”
Samson felt for the two middle pillars that held up the building. He leaned against them, one at his right hand and one at his left.

Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” Then he leaned with all his weight. The building came down on the rulers and on everyone inside. The people Samson killed as he died outnumbered the people he had killed while he lived.

His brothers and the rest of his father’s household went down to fetch him. They carried him home and laid him in the grave of his father Manoah, between Zorah and Eshtaol. Samson had led Israel for twenty years.

notes.text: Sorek means “choice vine.” The Greek Old Testament (B text) keeps the Hebrew as a name (Alsorech). The A text reads “the brook of Sorek.”
The meaning of Delilah is not certain. It may come from dallah, “hair, threads,” or from dalal, “to be weak or small.”
Probably shekels. Eleven hundred shekels weighed about 28 pounds (12.6 kilograms, kg). Hebrew “a thousand and a hundred of silver.”
Or “cords” or “sinews.” Hebrew yetarim was used for bowstrings and tent cords.

The Hebrew here seems shorter than it should be, perhaps because a copyist’s eye skipped between similar words. The Greek Old Testament has a longer text: “If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten them with the pin into the wall, then I shall become weak and be like any other man.” And in verse 14: “And while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web.”
Or “to hurt” or “to overpower.” The Greek Old Testament reads “and she began to make him weak.” Some scholars read “he began to grow weak.”
Dagon was a grain or storm god. People in Mesopotamia, Syria, and Philistia worshiped him.

verses.text: In the hill country of Ephraim there was a man called Micah.{a}

Micah said to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver{b} that went missing from you, the ones you cursed over while I was listening, are here with me. I took them.” “Yahweh bless you, my son,” she answered.

Micah gave back the eleven hundred pieces to his mother. She said, “From my own hand I now give this silver to Yahweh, for the good of my son. It will pay for an idol carved from wood and an idol cast from metal. Take it back, then.”
When Micah returned the silver to her, she took two hundred pieces and gave them to a silversmith, who turned them into a carved idol and a cast one. They stood in Micah’s house.
Micah owned a shrine.{c} He had an ephod and some household gods{d} made, and he installed{e} one of his sons as priest.
At that time Israel had no king. Everyone did whatever seemed right to him.
A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, of the Judah clan, was living in that town as a stranger.
He left the town of Bethlehem to find some other place to stay. As he traveled, he reached Micah’s house in the hills of Ephraim.
Micah asked, “Where are you from?” “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah,” the young man said, “and I am searching for a home.”
Micah said, “Stay here with me. Be a father and a priest to me, and every year I will pay you ten pieces of silver,{f} a set of clothes, and your meals.” The Levite went in.
He agreed to stay with Micah, and the young man became like one of Micah’s own sons.
Micah put the Levite in office, and the young man served as his priest and lived at Micah’s place.
Micah said, “Now I am sure Yahweh will treat me well, for a Levite serves as my priest.”

notes.text: Micah (here Hebrew Mikayehu, in verses 1 and 4; elsewhere Mikah) means “Who is like Yahweh?”
Probably shekels. Eleven hundred shekels weighed about 28 pounds (12.6 kilograms, kg). The two hundred pieces in verse 4 weighed about 5 pounds (2.3 kg).
Hebrew “a house of God” (or “of gods”).
Hebrew teraphim, small household idols. They may also have been used to learn the future.
Hebrew “filled the hand of,” a saying for putting a priest in office. It is also used in verse 12.
Probably shekels. Ten shekels weighed about 4 ounces (115 grams, g).

verses.text: In those days Israel had no king. The tribe of Dan was searching for land to settle, since until then no share had come to them among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites chose five strong men from their families in Zorah and Eshtaol to spy out the land and explore it. “Go and explore the land,” they told them. The men came to the hill country of Ephraim and stayed the night at Micah’s house.
When they were near Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. They stopped and asked him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?”
He told them, “Micah hired me. I am his priest, and he pays me.”
They said, “Ask God for us. We want to know if this trip of ours will succeed.”
The priest said, “Go in peace. Yahweh is with you on your trip.”

The five men journeyed on and reached Laish. They saw that the people there felt safe, just like the Sidonians. They were peaceful and trusting. Nothing was lacking in that land, and the people were wealthy.{a} They lived far from Sidon and had no treaty with anyone else.{b}
When the five men came back to their relatives in Zorah and Eshtaol, the relatives asked, “What did you find?”
They said, “Let us march against them! We have seen the land, and it is very good. Why do you sit here doing nothing? Do not delay. Go in and take it.
You will find a people who suspect nothing and a land that is wide open. God has given it to you. It has everything anyone could want.”
Six hundred men of the tribe of Dan, armed for war, marched out of Zorah and Eshtaol.
On the way they camped near Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why the place is still called Mahaneh-dan.{c} Its location is west{d} of Kiriath-jearim.
They traveled on to Ephraim’s hill country and reached Micah’s house.
The five men who had gone to spy out Laish said to their relatives, “Do you know what is in one of these houses? An ephod, some household gods, a carved idol, and a cast idol! Decide what to do.”
They left the road and went to the house where the young Levite stayed, which was Micah’s house, and asked how he was.
The six hundred Danite soldiers, with their weapons ready, took their place at the gate’s entrance.
Meanwhile the five spies went in and removed the carved idol, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast idol. The priest was standing at the gate’s entrance with the six hundred soldiers.
When the five men entered Micah’s house and carried off the carved idol, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast idol, the priest said, “What do you think you are doing?”
They answered, “Hush! Cover your mouth. Come along with us and be our father and priest. Which is better, serving the household of one man or serving a whole tribe, a whole family of Israel?”
The priest was glad. He picked up the ephod, the household gods, and the carved idol and joined the crowd.
They turned around and set out, with the little children, the animals, and their goods in the lead.
They were already far from Micah’s house when the men of the nearby houses were gathered, and they overtook the Danites.
Shouting, they made the Danites turn around. Then they asked Micah, “What has come over you? Why did you call out all these men?”
Micah said, “You have taken my gods, the ones I made, and my priest, and you are leaving. What is left for me? How can you ask, ‘What is wrong?’”
The men of Dan said, “Watch your tongue. Some of the men with us are quick to anger. They could attack you, and then you and your family would lose your lives.”
So the men of Dan went on. Micah could see they were stronger than he was. He turned back and went to his house.

The Danites carried away the idols Micah had made, along with his priest. They reached Laish, a peaceful people who did not suspect an attack. They struck them down with swords and set the town on fire.
No one came to the rescue. Laish was far from Sidon, and its people had no dealings with others. The town stood in the valley of Beth-rehob. The Danites rebuilt it and settled there.
They gave it the name Dan, after their forefather Dan, a son of Israel. Before that, the town’s name had been Laish.

The Danites put up the carved idol for themselves. Jonathan, a son of Gershom and grandson of Moses,{e} and then his sons, acted as priests for the tribe of Dan until the day the land was carried off into captivity.{f}
They kept the carved idol that Micah had made for as long as God’s house stood at Shiloh.

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew in this part is not certain.

This follows the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament (B text). The A text, which some scholars follow, reads “with Aram” (Syria). In Hebrew the two words differ by one letter (adam, “anyone,” and aram).
Mahaneh-dan means “camp of Dan.”
Hebrew “behind,” meaning west.

Most Hebrew manuscripts read “Manasseh,” but the letter n (nun) is written above the line, raised between the other letters. It is the only raised nun in the Hebrew Bible. Without it the word reads “Moses.” Jewish tradition (the Talmud, Bava Batra 109b) says the scribes added the nun to spare Moses the shame of a grandson who served as a priest of idols, while showing that it was an addition. The Greek Old Testament A text and the Latin Vulgate read “Moses.” The B text reads “Manasseh.” Gershom was the son of Moses (Exodus 2:22).

This follows the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament. Some scholars change the Hebrew slightly to read “the captivity of the ark” (compare 1 Samuel 4:11, 21-22). The captivity of the land may mean the Assyrian deportations in 734-732 B.C. or 722 B.C.

subheads.1: The Tribe of Dan Looks for Land

verses.text: In those days Israel had no king. A Levite lived far back in the hills of Ephraim. He took as his secondary wife a woman from Bethlehem in Judah.
She grew angry with him{a} and left. She went back to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah and stayed there four months.

Her husband went after her to speak kindly to her and bring her home. His servant and two donkeys went with him. She led him into her father’s house, and the girl’s father was delighted at the sight of him.
The young woman’s father, the Levite’s father-in-law, begged him to stay. So he stayed three days with them. They ate and drank, and he slept there.
On the fourth day they rose early, and the Levite made ready to go. But the girl’s father told his son-in-law, “Eat a bit of bread first, to build up your strength. Then go on your way.”
The two men sat down to a meal and drank together. Afterward the girl’s father urged, “Be my guest one more night. Make yourself comfortable.”
The Levite stood to go, but his father-in-law kept pleading, and so he lodged there yet another night.
When the fifth day dawned, he got up early to go. The girl’s father said, “Have a bite to eat first. Hold off until the sun is high.” So the two men ate together.

Then the man stood up to go with his wife and servant. But his father-in-law said, “Look, the day is almost over, and evening is near. Stay another night. The sun is going down. Rest here and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can start early and go home.”
But the man would not stay another night. He set out and came as far as the place opposite Jebus (which is Jerusalem). He had his two saddled donkeys and his wife with him.
They were near Jebus, and the day was almost gone. The servant said to his master, “Let us stop at this town of the Jebusites and spend the night.”
His master said, “No. We will not turn aside to a town of foreigners, where no Israelites live. We will go on to Gibeah.”
He added, “Come, let us try to get to Gibeah or Ramah, and stay in one or the other.”
They walked on, and the sun went down just as they reached Gibeah, a town of the tribe of Benjamin.
They stopped there for the night. The Levite went into the town and sat down in the open square, but nobody invited them home.
Toward evening an old man came walking in from a day’s work in the fields. His home had been in the hills of Ephraim, but now he lived in Gibeah, where the local people belonged to Benjamin.
The old man noticed the traveler sitting in the square. “Where are you going?” he asked. “Where did you come from?”

The man answered, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the far hills of Ephraim, where I live. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am on my way to the house of Yahweh.{b} But no one has taken me in.
We have straw and feed for the donkeys, and bread and wine for me, your servant woman, and the young man with us. We need nothing more.”
“Peace to you,” said the old man. “Let me take care of whatever you need. Only, never spend the night out in the square.”
He led them inside and fed the donkeys. The guests rinsed their feet, then sat down to eat and drink.

They were enjoying the meal when some wicked men{c} of the town closed in around the house. They beat on the door and called to the old man, the owner, “Send out the man who is staying with you. Our wish is to have sex with him.”
So the old man went out to them. “No, my brothers, I beg you, do not be so wicked. This man is my guest. Do not commit this terrible act.
Look, here is my daughter, who has never been with a man, and the man’s wife. Let me bring them out. Do with them as you please. But this man is my guest. Do nothing so terrible to him.”
The men would not listen to him. So the Levite seized his wife and pushed her out to them. They abused her all night, until morning, and when the sun came up they let her go.
As the day began to dawn, the woman crawled back and collapsed at the door of the house where her husband was staying. She lay there until it was light.
Her husband got up that morning and opened the door to continue his trip. There lay his wife at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
“Get up,” he said. “Let us go.” But there was no answer.{d} He loaded her onto his donkey and started the trip home.
Back at his house, he took a knife, cut her body into twelve pieces, and sent a piece to each part of Israel.
All who saw it said, “Never since the day Israel left Egypt has such a thing been done or seen. Think it over! Talk it through, and say what should be done!”

notes.text: Hebrew “played the prostitute against him” (zanah). Some Greek manuscripts read “was angry with him,” perhaps from a different Hebrew verb. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “left him.”
This follows the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament reads “to my house,” which fits verse 29. The Hebrew may come from a misread short form.
Hebrew beliya’al, “worthlessness.”
The Greek Old Testament adds “because she was dead.”

verses.text: Then all the Israelites came out, from Dan to Beersheba, together with the people of Gilead. As one body they met before Yahweh at Mizpah.
The heads of every tribe of Israel took their places in the meeting of God’s people. They counted four hundred thousand{a} soldiers on foot who carried swords.
The Benjaminites heard that Israel’s people had gone up to Mizpah. “Tell us,” the Israelites said, “how did this evil thing come about?”
The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, said, “My wife and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
In the night the leaders of Gibeah rose against me and closed in on the house, meaning to kill me. They abused my wife until she died.
I cut her body into pieces and sent them through all the land Israel owns, because these men have done a shameful and terrible thing in Israel.
All you Israelites, speak up! Give your advice.”
All the people rose together and made a vow: “Not one of us will walk to his tent. Not one of us will turn toward his house.
This is what we will do to Gibeah. We will go up against it, choosing men by lot.

From all the tribes of Israel we will take ten men out of every hundred, a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to bring food for the army. When the army comes to Gibeah of Benjamin, it will pay them back for the shameful thing they did in Israel.”
So all the men of Israel gathered against the town, joined together as one.
The tribes of Israel sent messengers to all the families of Benjamin. “What is this evil thing that happened among you?” they asked.
“Hand over those wicked men in Gibeah. We will put them to death and clear this evil out of Israel.” But Benjamin refused to listen to their own brothers, the other Israelites.
They came together from their towns to Gibeah to go out and fight the Israelites.
That day the Benjaminites counted twenty-six thousand{b} men with swords from their towns. They also counted seven hundred chosen men from Gibeah.
Among all these soldiers were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed.{c} Each of them could throw a stone at a hair and not miss.
The Israelites, not counting Benjamin, counted four hundred thousand men with swords, every one of them a trained soldier.
The Israelites set out for Bethel and asked God, “Who among us should lead the attack on Benjamin?” Yahweh answered, “Judah first.”
In the morning the Israelites broke camp and settled in across from Gibeah.
Israel’s men went out to battle Benjamin and formed lines in front of Gibeah.
The Benjaminites rushed out of Gibeah and killed twenty-two thousand Israelites on the field that day.
But the Israelites took heart and lined up again in the same place as on the first day.
They went up and wept before Yahweh until evening. They asked him, “Shall we fight our relatives, the Benjaminites, again?” Yahweh said, “Go up against them.”
So the Israelites came near to Benjamin on the second day.
This time the Benjaminites came out of Gibeah to meet them and struck down eighteen thousand more Israelites. All of these were swordsmen.
Then all the Israelites, the entire army, went up to Bethel and wept there. They sat before Yahweh and ate nothing all day until evening. They brought burnt offerings and peace offerings to Yahweh.
The Israelites asked Yahweh a question. (The chest of the covenant of God was there in those days,

and Phinehas, a son of Eleazar and a grandson of Aaron, was serving in front of it.) They asked, “Should we go out to fight our relatives, the Benjaminites, one more time, or should we stop?” Yahweh answered, “Go! Tomorrow they will be yours.”
Then Israel hid soldiers around Gibeah, waiting to spring a trap.
On the third day the Israelites went up against Benjamin and took up their places at Gibeah as on the earlier days.

The Benjaminites came out to fight and were drawn off, away from the town. As before, they began to cut down Israelites along the roads, one leading up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and out in the fields. About thirty Israelites fell.
The Benjaminites thought, “We are winning, as we did the first time.” But the Israelites had a plan: “We will run away so that they chase us from the town out onto the roads.”
All the men of Israel left their places and took up new ones at Baal-tamar.{d} Then the men in ambush charged from their hiding place west of Geba.{e}
Ten thousand chosen men from all Israel attacked Gibeah. The fighting was heavy, but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was near.
Yahweh gave Israel the win over Benjamin. That day the Israelites struck down 25,100 Benjaminite swordsmen.
Then the Benjaminites saw they were beaten. The Israelites had given ground to them, for they were relying on the men they had hidden near Gibeah.
The ambush force dashed into Gibeah, spread out, and put everyone in the town to the sword.
The Israelites had agreed on a signal with the men in ambush: they would send up a great cloud of smoke from the town.
When the smoke went up, the Israelites would turn in the battle. Benjamin had begun to strike down about thirty Israelites. They told themselves, “We are winning, just as in the first fight!”
But when the cloud of smoke began to rise from the town, the Benjaminites looked behind them. The whole town was going up in flames toward the sky.
Then the Israelites turned, and the Benjaminites were filled with terror, for they saw that disaster had come upon them.
They ran from the Israelites toward the desert, but the fighting stayed with them. Men from the towns were also cutting them down in the middle of it.
They surrounded the Benjaminites, pressed after them, and trampled them down from Nohah{f} to the east side of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand Benjaminites died, all of them fighters.
The others turned and ran for the desert, toward the rock of Rimmon. Israel picked off five thousand along the roads.{g} Still the Israelites pursued, as far as Gidom, where two thousand more fell.
So that day twenty-five thousand Benjaminites who carried swords fell, all of them brave men.
But six hundred men turned and fled into the desert. They reached the rock of Rimmon, and there they stayed four months.
The Israelites went back to the rest of Benjamin and killed them with the sword, the people of every town, the animals, and everything they found. They also set fire to every town they came to.

notes.text: The Hebrew word elef, “thousand,” can sometimes mean a family group or army unit rather than an exact number. The numbers are given here as written. This applies to the whole chapter.
This follows the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament (B text) reads “twenty-three thousand.” Compare verses 35 and 46.
Hebrew “bound in the right hand,” as in 3:15. The Greek Old Testament reads “able to use both hands alike.”
Baal-tamar means “lord of the palm tree.”
Maareh-geba probably means “the open area of Geba (or Gibeah).” The Hebrew is not certain. The Greek Old Testament keeps it as a name.
Or “from their resting place.” Hebrew menuhah. The Greek Old Testament reads “from Nua.”
Hebrew “gleaned,” meaning picked off one by one, like gleanings.

subheads.12: Benjamin Will Not Give Up the Guilty Men

verses.text: Back at Mizpah the Israelites had sworn an oath: “No one among us will let his daughter marry a Benjaminite.”
The people went to Bethel and sat in front of God till evening. They wept loudly and bitterly.
“Yahweh, God of Israel,” they cried, “why has this come upon Israel? Today a whole tribe is gone from us!”
The next day, at dawn, the people built an altar and brought burnt offerings and peace offerings.

The Israelites asked, “Was there any tribe of Israel that did not come up with the rest to the assembly before Yahweh?” They had sworn a serious oath. Anyone who failed to come to Yahweh at Mizpah must die.
The Israelites grieved over Benjamin, their brother. “A whole tribe has been cut off from Israel today,” they said.
“What can we do about wives for the men who survived? We took an oath in Yahweh’s name not to give them any of our daughters.”
So they asked, “Which tribe of Israel did not come to Yahweh at Mizpah?” It turned out that Jabesh-gilead had sent no one to the assembly in the camp.
When the people were counted, not one person from Jabesh-gilead was there.
So the community sent twelve thousand of their best fighters. Their orders were: “Go and put the people of Jabesh-gilead to the sword, women and children too.
Here is your task. Kill all the men, and kill every woman who has been with a man.”{a}
In Jabesh-gilead the soldiers found four hundred girls who had never slept with a man. They took them to the camp at Shiloh in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole community sent a message to the Benjaminites at the rock of Rimmon, offering them peace.
So Benjamin returned, and the Israelites gave them the women of Jabesh-gilead who had been spared. Still, the number fell short.{b}
The people grieved over Benjamin, because Yahweh had torn a hole in the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the community asked, “What shall we do about wives for the survivors? The women of Benjamin have been killed.”
They said, “Those who escaped from Benjamin must have land of their own. Then no tribe will be wiped out of Israel.
But we cannot give them our daughters as wives.” The Israelites had sworn, “Cursed is anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin.”
Then they remembered, “Every year Yahweh has a festival at Shiloh.{c} That town sits north of Bethel and south of Lebonah, beside the highway that runs from Bethel to Shechem on its east side.”
They gave these orders to the Benjaminites: “Go and lie in wait among the vineyards.
Watch for the girls of Shiloh to come out and dance. Then rush from the vineyards. Each of you must grab a girl for his wife and hurry back to Benjamin’s land.

If their fathers or brothers come to us and object, we will tell them: ‘Do us the kindness of letting these men keep them. We did not take wives for each of them during the war. And since you did not hand your daughters over yourselves, you are not guilty.’”{d}
The Benjaminites did so. From the dancers they snatched as many wives as they needed. Then they went home to their own land, rebuilt their towns, and settled in them.
The Israelites then left and went home, each man to his own tribe and family, to the land that was his share.
In those days Israel had no king. Everyone did whatever seemed right to him.

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament adds “but you must keep the virgins alive. And they did so.”
Hebrew “but they did not find enough for them.” The Greek Old Testament reads “and this pleased them.”

This was probably the autumn Festival of Booths (Tabernacles), held at the end of the grape harvest in the seventh month (September to October). Compare the vineyards in verses 20-21. This is not certain.
The meaning of the Hebrew is not certain. The Greek manuscripts differ in this verse.
